title: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Coil
short_intro: The magnetic field at any axial point of a current-carrying circular coil is directed along its axis and is derived using the Biot-Savart law. It forms the foundation for calculating magnetic fields of complex winding geometries in electrical machines.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of magnetic field at the center and axial points of a circular coil, variation of field with distance, and application of the Right-Hand Rule.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of the axial field formula using Biot-Savart law, spatial second derivative of the field, Helmholtz coil configuration for uniform magnetic field, and integration over multiple turns.

prerequisites: Biot-Savart Law and its vector form
Right-hand thumb and palm rules for magnetic fields

concept_notes.heading: Biot-Savart Law Application to a Circular Loop
bullets: Consider a circular coil of radius R carrying current I with N turns, lying in the y-z plane with its center at the origin.
An elemental current length Idl is perpendicular to the position vector r connecting the element to an axial point P at distance x.
By the Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB due to Idl is independent of the azimuthal angle around the loop by symmetry.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry and Vector Components
bullets: The magnetic field vector dB makes an angle with the axis of the coil due to the cross product in the Biot-Savart law.
Perpendicular components (dB_y) cancel out diametrically opposite elements, leaving only the axial components (dB_x) to contribute to the net magnetic field.
The net magnetic field is directed entirely along the axis of the coil (the x-axis).

concept_notes.heading: Special Case: Center of the Coil
bullets: At the center of the circular coil, the axial distance x becomes zero.
The general axial formula reduces to the maximum field value at the center: B = \mu_0 N I / (2R).
The field lines are straight and parallel near the center, representing a uniform magnetic field over a small region.

concept_notes.heading: Inflection Points and Helmholtz Coils
bullets: The derivative of the axial magnetic field vanishes at x = \pm R/2, which correspond to points of inflection where the field gradient is maximum.
When two identical coaxial coils are separated by a distance equal to their radius R, their combined field has a region of high uniformity between them, known as a Helmholtz coil setup.
In a Helmholtz coil, the first and second spatial derivatives of the magnetic field vanish at the midpoint, ensuring uniform magnetic field distribution.

derivations.title: Derivation of Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Coil
derivations.conditions: Coil of radius R, N turns, current I, point P at axial distance x.
steps: Write the Biot-Savart law for a current element Idl: dB = (\mu_0 / 4\pi) * (I |dl \times r|) / r^3.
Recognize that angle between dl and r is 90 degrees, so |dl \times r| = dl * r.
Substitute r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}, giving dB = (\mu_0 I dl) / (4\pi (R^2 + x^2)).
Resolve dB into axial (dB cos\theta) and radial (dB sin\theta) components, where cos\theta = R / \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}.
Integrate dB cos\theta around the loop: B = \int dB (R / \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}) = (\mu_0 I R / 4\pi (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}) \int dl.
Since \int dl = 2\pi R for a single turn and multiplying by N turns, obtain the final result.

derivations.title: Derivation of Position of Inflection Points (d2B/dx2 = 0)
derivations.conditions: Single circular coil of radius R, finding points where curvature of B(x) changes sign.
steps: Start with B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}.
Find the first derivative dB/dx = -\frac{3 \mu_0 I R^2 x}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{5/2}}.
Apply the quotient rule to find the second derivative d^2B/dx^2 = -\frac{3 \mu_0 I R^2}{2} * \frac{(R^2 + x^2)^{5/2} - x * (5/2)(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}(2x)}{(R^2 + x^2)^5}.
Simplify the numerator by factoring out (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}: numerator proportional to (R^2 + x^2) - 5x^2 = R^2 - 4x^2.
Set d^2B/dx^2 = 0 to solve for x: R^2 - 4x^2 = 0.

formula_sheet.name: Axial Magnetic Field of Circular Coil
formula_sheet.variables: B = Magnetic field, \mu_0 = Permeability of free space, N = Number of turns, I = Current, R = Radius, x = Axial distance
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for a tightly wound circular coil of radius R

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic Field at the Center
formula_sheet.variables: B_{center} = Field at x=0, N = Number of turns, I = Current, R = Radius
formula_sheet.conditions: At the geometric center of the coil

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic Field at Large Distances (x >> R)
formula_sheet.equation_html: B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2x^3} = \frac{\mu_0 2 M}{4\pi x^3}
formula_sheet.variables: M = NIA = Magnetic dipole moment of the coil, x = Distance
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid when axial distance x is much greater than radius R

formula_sheet.name: Helmholtz Coil Magnetic Field
formula_sheet.variables: B_{total} = Combined field at the midpoint, separation d = R
formula_sheet.conditions: Two identical coaxial coils separated by distance equal to their radius

formula_sheet.name: First Derivative of Axial Field
formula_sheet.variables: Rate of change of magnetic field along the axis

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic Dipole Moment of Coil
formula_sheet.equation_html: M = N I A = N I \pi R^2
formula_sheet.variables: M = Magnetic moment, A = Area of cross section

formula_sheet.name: Ratio of Field at Distance x to Center Field

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of B with Axial Distance x
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped symmetrical curve centered at x = 0, with maximum value B_0 at origin, inflection points at x = \pm R/2 where curvature changes, and asymptotic approach to zero as x approaches infinity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that the magnetic field is maximum at the center and drops off non-linearly with distance, falling rapidly when x exceeds R.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in multiple-choice questions to identify inflection points (x = R/2) and the general shape of the decay curve.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Helmholtz Coil Uniform Field Region
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two individual bell-shaped curves overlapping such that their inflection points coincide, resulting in a nearly flat-topped resultant magnetic field curve in the central region.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how combining two coils at a separation equal to their radius produces a region of nearly constant magnetic field strength.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on achieving uniform magnetic fields in laboratories.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Field Lines around a Circular Coil
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Closed loops emerging through the center of the coil, looping around the conductor wire, densely packed at the center and spreading out further away.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the direction and density of the magnetic flux, confirming the magnetic dipole behavior of the current loop.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Pattern identification and matching questions in TGT and PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: A circular coil of 100 turns has a radius of 0.1 m and carries a current of 2 A. Calculate the magnetic field at its center.
solution_steps: Identify given values: N = 100, R = 0.1 m, I = 2 A, \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} T m A^{-1}.
Use formula for field at the center: B = \mu_0 N I / (2R).

solved_numericals.question: At what distance along the axis of a circular coil of radius R is the magnetic field equal to 1/8th of its value at the center?
solution_steps: Use ratio formula: B(x) / B(0) = (R^2 / (R^2 + x^2))^{3/2}.
Take the 2/3 power on both sides: (1/8)^{2/3} = R^2 / (R^2 + x^2), which gives 1/4 = R^2 / (R^2 + x^2).
Cross multiply: R^2 + x^2 = 4R^2, so x^2 = 3R^2.

solved_numericals.question: Two identical coaxial circular coils each of radius 0.5 m and 50 turns are placed 0.5 m apart. If a current of 1 A flows through both in the same direction, find the magnetic field at the midpoint between them.
solution_steps: Identify that the separation d equals the radius R (0.5 m), which satisfies the Helmholtz coil condition.
Use the Helmholtz coil formula: B_{total} = (4/5)^{3/2} * (\mu_0 N I / R) * 2 (since there are two identical coils).
Calculate single coil center field: (4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 50) / 0.5 = 4\pi \times 10^{-5} T.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the coil wire is thin and the current is uniformly distributed across its cross-section.
Edge effects and finite thickness of wire insulation are neglected in standard academic derivations.
Formula assumes free space or non-magnetic medium (\mu_r \approx 1) unless explicitly modified by core permeability.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The magnetic field is maximum at points other than the center along the axis.
common_misconceptions.correct: The magnetic field is always maximum at the center (x = 0) of a circular current-carrying coil.
common_misconceptions.why: The denominator (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} is minimum when x = 0, making the field magnitude maximum at the center.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Radial components of the magnetic field do not exist anywhere on the axis.
common_misconceptions.correct: Radial components cancel out strictly along the axis due to symmetry, but exist off-axis.
common_misconceptions.why: Diametrically opposite current elements produce radial components that cancel out only on the symmetrical central axis.

quick_revision: Axial magnetic field formula: B = \mu_0 N I R^2 / 2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}.
Axial Magnetic Field of Circular Coil: B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}
Magnetic Field at the Center: B_{center} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}
